chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ahmad ibn Al-Hasan Al-Mithammi, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu Al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'I threw something at a man, the like of which does not kill (but he dies)?' He said: 'This is erroneous (killing).' Then he picked up a small pebble and threw it. I said, 'I threw it at a sheep but it hit a man?' He said: 'This is the error in which there is no doubt, and the deliberate is that which he strikes with something, the like of which could kill.'

key_terms.الْعَمْدُ: Deliberate killing (intentional killing with a typically lethal object)
key_terms.خَطَأٌ: Erroneous killing (killing by mistake or with a non-lethal object)
key_terms.يُقْتَلُ بِمِثْلِهِ: Killed by its like (indicating typical lethality)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between deliberate and erroneous killing in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between deliberate homicide and accidental killing by using the tangible example of throwing a stone, establishing that the lethality of the instrument and the intent determine the classification. This hadith is foundational in Shia fiqh for determining diyya (blood money) and qisas (retaliation), emphasizing that using a non-lethal object to kill a person constitutes error, whereas using a typically lethal object constitutes deliberate action. The narrative underscores the practical application of legal principles in everyday actions, linking physical causality with legal culpability.
